summary.title: The reference product
points: A generic relies on a reference product authorised in the EU on a complete dossier of its own.
Art. 10(2)(b): same active substances and amounts, same pharmaceutical form, bioequivalence.
Salts, esters and isomers count as the same substance unless safety or efficacy differ significantly; all immediate-release oral forms count as one form.
The reference can be authorised in another EU country (European reference product).
Global marketing authorisation: later strengths and forms don't restart the protection clock.

exercises.scenario: Your generic is a capsule; the reference product is a film-coated tablet. Both are immediate-release.

questions.prompt: Is the pharmaceutical form 'the same' in the legal sense?
options: Only if the reference holder agrees in writing
Only if the capsule's colour and size match the tablet
No: a capsule and a tablet always need a hybrid application
Yes: immediate-release oral forms count as one form
questions.explanation: Art. 10(2)(b) treats them as one pharmaceutical form.

questions.prompt: Your API is a different salt of the same substance. What decides if it's 'the same active substance'?
options: Whether safety or efficacy differ significantly
Whether the reference holder has approved the new salt in writing
Whether the salt has its own patent
Whether the same supplier makes both
questions.explanation: If they differ significantly, extra data are needed.

exercises.scenario: The originator added a 5 mg strength six years after first approval. Sales asks if that delays the 5 mg generic.

questions.prompt: When does protection for the 5 mg strength start?
options: When the 5 mg strength itself was approved, six years later
When the 5 mg strength was first sold in your country
At the product's first EU authorisation
It has no protection, as an added strength
questions.explanation: Global marketing authorisation, Art. 6(1).

questions.prompt: The reference isn't sold in your filing country. Can you still file?
options: No, it must be on the market in every filing country
Yes, naming a reference authorised in another EU state
Only after the reference holder withdraws elsewhere
Only through the centralised procedure, never in a DCP or MRP
questions.explanation: The European reference product rule, Art. 10(1).

summary.title: Bioequivalence
points: BE shows the generic releases the substance at the same rate and extent as the reference.
Usually healthy volunteers in a crossover design, with blood samples over time.
Cmax is the peak (speed); AUC is the total exposure (amount).
Test: the 90% CI of the generic/reference ratio within 80.00–125.00% for AUC and Cmax.
Narrow-index substances: 90.00–111.11%; highly variable: Cmax can widen up to 69.84–143.19%. A failed study costs months.

exercises.scenario: A BE report shows an AUC ratio of 97% with a 90% CI of 91–104%, and a Cmax ratio of 108% with a CI of 96–127%.

questions.prompt: Does the study pass under the usual test?
options: No: the Cmax interval goes above 125%
Yes: only AUC has to fall within the range
No: the AUC ratio should be exactly 100%
Yes: both point estimates sit between 80% and 125%
questions.explanation: Both intervals must lie within 80.00–125.00%.

questions.prompt: What's a typical response?
options: Switch to Art. 10a well-established use
Reformulate or run a larger study
File anyway and explain the result in the clinical overview
Repeat the same study on the same batches
questions.explanation: Either way, months of delay and often a new batch.

exercises.scenario: A buyer worries that '80–125%' means the generic may deliver 20% less drug.

questions.prompt: What do you tell them?
options: Yes: a generic may deliver up to 20% less, which is why it's cheaper to make
Only for narrow-index substances, which use a wider range
The range is for the uncertainty, and averages sit near 100%
The range applies only to Cmax, not to total exposure
questions.explanation: What must fit is the confidence interval around the average.

questions.prompt: Which substances can use a tightened 90.00–111.11% range?
options: Any substance filed under Art. 8(3)
Highly variable substances
Substances in fixed combinations
Narrow-therapeutic-index substances
questions.explanation: Small changes matter clinically for them.

summary.title: Biowaivers
points: A biowaiver allows skipping an in-vivo BE study, justified with lab data.
Additional strengths: same process, same qualitative composition, proportional composition, similar dissolution, linear pharmacokinetics.
Which strength must be studied depends on the substance.
BCS-based waiver (ICH M9): mainly highly soluble, immediate-release substances meeting strict criteria.
Both rest on dissolution testing, usually at several pH levels.

exercises.scenario: Your generic comes in 10, 20 and 40 mg. The BE study was done on 40 mg. The 10 mg tablet uses a different binder.

questions.prompt: Can the additional-strength waiver cover 10 mg?
options: Probably not: the qualitative composition differs
Yes: one study always covers every strength
Yes, if the 10 mg tablet dissolves faster
Only if the 10 mg is the strength most often prescribed
questions.explanation: All five conditions must be met, including the same qualitative composition.

questions.prompt: Which lab test do both waiver types depend on?
options: Stability testing at 40 °C
Microbial limits testing
Particle-size analysis of the API
Dissolution testing
questions.explanation: The waiver stands or falls on those comparisons.

exercises.scenario: A partner says 'we have a BCS waiver, so no BE study at all'.

questions.prompt: When is that plausible?
options: Any substance with a narrow therapeutic index
Any substance in a modified-release form
A highly soluble substance in an immediate-release form meeting ICH M9
Any substance at all, as long as the product is made at an EU site with GMP
questions.explanation: Less common, but very valuable when it applies.

questions.prompt: Why should the PM ask early which strength carries the BE study?
options: It decides which strength launches first in each country
It decides whether the others need their own studies, which costs months
Because the authority only assesses the studied strength and approves the rest automatically
It sets the order of the strengths on the carton
questions.explanation: Waivers save months and money only if documented.

summary.title: Data and market protection
points: Data protection: generics can't refer to the originator's data, so they can't file.
Market protection: generics may be approved but can't be sold.
Today, 8 + 2 (+1): file from year 8, launch from year 10, or 11 with a significant new indication.
Pharma package: 8 years of data protection plus 1 of market protection, extensions capped at 11; applicable around 2028.
Launch date is the latest of filing end, market protection end and patent/SPC expiry.

exercises.scenario: A reference product was first authorised in the EU in March 2018. No new indication was added.

questions.prompt: When may a generic be filed?
options: March 2026
As soon as the patent expires
March 2029
March 2028
questions.explanation: 8 years of data protection.

questions.prompt: When may it be placed on the market, ignoring patents?
options: Immediately after approval
March 2028
March 2026
March 2029
questions.explanation: 10 years; 11 only with a significant new indication.

exercises.scenario: A colleague says 'the reform cuts market protection to 1 year, so plan our 2027 launches on that'.

questions.prompt: What should you plan with?
options: Whichever gives the earliest date
The new 8 + 1, since political agreement makes it law
8 + 0, since the Bolar exemption is widened
Today's 8 + 2 (+1), until RA confirms otherwise
questions.explanation: It applies only after adoption and transition, around 2028.

questions.prompt: Why do many teams file around year 8?
options: So they can launch at year 8, as soon as data protection ends
Because filing earlier would breach the patent
So approval lands just as market protection ends
Because data protection ends at year 10
questions.explanation: Filing can and should start before launch is allowed.

summary.title: The legal bases
points: The legal basis is the article of Directive 2001/83/EC the application uses; it decides what data are needed.
10(1) generic; 10(3) hybrid for differences or when BE isn't enough; 10a well-established use.
10b fixed combination; 10c informed consent; 8(3) full or mixed dossier.
RA owns the decision; get it in writing before fixing the timeline.
A late switch, say generic to hybrid, means new studies and months of delay.

exercises.scenario: Your company wants an oral solution, but the reference product exists only as tablets.

questions.prompt: Which basis is most likely?
options: Art. 10a well-established use
Art. 10(1) generic
Art. 10(3) hybrid
Art. 10c informed consent
questions.explanation: A different form means bridging data on top of the reference.

questions.prompt: What does the hybrid add to the reference data?
options: A full clinical programme from scratch
Bridging studies
Published literature only
Nothing beyond the quality data
questions.explanation: It relies on the reference plus bridging data.

exercises.scenario: Another MAH lets you use its full dossier for an identical product sold under your name.

questions.prompt: Which basis applies?
options: Art. 10c informed consent
Art. 10b fixed combination
Art. 8(3) full application
Art. 10(1) generic
questions.explanation: The holder consents to its dossier being used.

questions.prompt: A substance has been in well-established EU medical use for over 10 years. What can replace your own studies?
options: A bioequivalence study only
Nothing; own studies are always needed
The reference product's data, under Art. 10(1)
Published literature, under Art. 10a
questions.explanation: Well-established use relies on the literature.

summary.title: Art. 10b fixed combinations
points: 10b: known substances combined in a way not yet authorised together.
Needs new non-clinical or clinical data on the combination, not references on each substance; full quality data always.
A common element: BE of the combined tablet against the separate products.
If an authorised A+B exists and its protection has expired, an A+B generic under 10(1) is usually simpler.
Plan the study, reference batches of both single products, and reporting time before filing.

exercises.scenario: You plan a rosuvastatin + ezetimibe tablet. An authorised combination of the two already exists, out of protection.

questions.prompt: Which route is usually simpler?
options: Art. 10a, because both substances are well known
A generic of that combination under Art. 10(1)
Art. 10b, since it always applies to two substances
Art. 8(3), because combinations need a full dossier
questions.explanation: 10b is for when no usable A+B reference exists.

questions.prompt: If you used 10b instead, which study would you most likely need?
options: BE of the combined tablet against the separate products
No study, only literature
Separate BE studies of each substance against its originator only
A placebo-controlled outcomes trial
questions.explanation: It shows the combination behaves like the free combination.

exercises.scenario: A partner says their 10b dossier 'has no quality data because both substances are known'.

questions.prompt: What's wrong?
options: Nothing: known substances need no quality data
Quality data can be borrowed from the single products' dossiers
Full quality data on the new product are always required
Quality data are needed only for the more potent substance
questions.explanation: Quality is never borrowed.

questions.prompt: What does 10b not require?
options: Full quality data
Reference batches of the single products for the BE study
New data on the combination
References proving each single substance works
questions.explanation: The single substances are already well known.

summary.title: Art. 8(3) full and mixed dossiers
points: 8(3) is a complete dossier with the company's own data; used when there's no usable EU reference product.
Full: own studies in every module. Mixed: own studies plus published literature (Annex I).
The quality module (CTD Module 3) is always your own product, on every basis.
Most pre-submission work and most assessment questions.
For an in-licensed '8(3)' dossier, check in the gap analysis what it really contains.

exercises.scenario: You in-license a dossier labelled '8(3)'.

questions.prompt: What do you check during the gap analysis?
options: Whether it holds own studies or literature
Whether the reference product is still on the market
Whether the BE study used an EU reference batch
Nothing, since 8(3) dossiers are complete by definition
questions.explanation: Full and mixed dossiers look alike from the cover.

questions.prompt: What should you budget extra for in the plan?
options: A longer national phase
Extra stability batches only
A second BE study, which every 8(3) dossier requires
Clock-stop time to answer more questions
questions.explanation: 8(3) dossiers usually draw more questions.

exercises.scenario: A colleague says 'for a generic we borrow everything, so the manufacturer's paperwork matters less'.

questions.prompt: Which part is never borrowed?
options: The clinical overview
The quality module, CTD Module 3
The non-clinical summaries
The bioequivalence study
questions.explanation: It always describes your own product.

questions.prompt: So who supplies that quality documentation on every route?
options: The QPPV
The reference product holder
The manufacturer
The national authority
questions.explanation: Its gaps delay every route equally.

summary.title: What makes a generic
points: Same active substances and amounts, same form, bioequivalence with an EU reference product.
BE: 90% CI of AUC and Cmax ratios within 80–125%, tighter or wider in special cases.
Biowaivers spare studies for extra strengths or BCS cases, if dissolution data support them.
Protection: file at year 8, launch at year 10 (or 11), from the first EU authorisation.
Later strengths don't restart the clock; plan with 8 + 2 (+1) until the reform applies.

exercises.scenario: A partner offers a generic in 25 and 50 mg. The reference was first approved in the EU in June 2017, and the 25 mg strength was added in 2021.

questions.prompt: When could you file, ignoring patents?
options: June 2025
2029, eight years after the 25 mg strength
June 2028
June 2027
questions.explanation: Global marketing authorisation: the clock starts at the first approval.

questions.prompt: BE was run only on 50 mg. What covers 25 mg?
options: The reference holder's own 25 mg BE data
Nothing; every strength needs its own study
A BCS waiver, which covers any strength
An additional-strength biowaiver, if the five conditions hold
questions.explanation: Same process, composition, proportionality, dissolution, linear PK.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between data protection and market protection in one sentence each.
questions.modelAnswer: Data protection: generics can't refer to the originator's data, so they can't file (8 years). Market protection: generics may be approved but not sold (2 more years, or 3 with a significant new indication).

exercises.scenario: The BE study of your generic failed on Cmax.

questions.prompt: What does this mean for the timeline?
options: A short clock-stop to explain the result
A switch to a BCS waiver
Months of delay, often with a new batch
Nothing if AUC passed
questions.explanation: Reformulate or run a larger study.

questions.prompt: Which date doesn't change because of the failure?
options: The first sale date
The end of market protection
The filing date, which slips with the study
The approval date
questions.explanation: Protection dates are fixed by the reference product, not by your study.

summary.title: Choosing the legal basis
points: The basis decides what data are needed, so how long preparation takes.
Combinations: 10b with new combination data, or an A+B generic if a reference exists.
8(3): own complete dossier, full or mixed; most work and most questions.
Quality is never borrowed; confirm the basis in writing before fixing the plan.

exercises.scenario: Three projects land on your desk: (A) a copy of a tablet out of protection, (B) a new two-substance tablet with no A+B on the market, (C) a new oral solution of a tablet-only reference.

questions.prompt: Which bases fit A, B and C?
questions.explanation: Generic, fixed combination, hybrid.

questions.prompt: Which project probably has the longest work before filing?
options: All three take the same time
B, with new studies on the combination
C, because a solution is easier to make
A, because the reference is old
questions.explanation: 10b usually needs new studies, often BE against the separate products.

questions.prompt: What three questions do you ask on any new project?
questions.modelAnswer: What's the legal basis, and is it in writing? What's the reference product and when was it first authorised in the EU, so when can we file and launch? Which studies exist, and which still have to be done?

exercises.scenario: Halfway through, RA says BE alone won't support the generic, and switches the project to a hybrid.

questions.prompt: What's the timeline effect?
options: A shorter assessment, as hybrids are simpler
None, the dossier is the same
Only a new cover letter and an updated legal-basis form
Bridging studies and usually months before filing
questions.explanation: A late switch is one of the costliest surprises.

questions.prompt: Which dossier part stays exactly the same task in either case?
options: The quality module on your own product
The clinical overview
The reference product justification
The bridging data
questions.explanation: Quality is always your own.

summary.title: Generic basics: the whole picture
points: A generic matches an EU reference product in substance, amount and form, and proves bioequivalence.
BE: 90% CI within 80–125% for AUC and Cmax; biowaivers can spare extra strengths.
File at year 8, launch at year 10 (or 11), counted from the first EU authorisation.
The legal basis (10(1), 10(3), 10a, 10b, 10c, 8(3)) sets the data and the preparation time.
Quality is never borrowed; it comes from the manufacturer on every route.
Late changes of basis or failed studies cost months.

exercises.scenario: BD proposes a generic of a reference first approved in the EU in October 2018, in three strengths, from an Indian partner.

questions.prompt: Earliest filing and launch dates, ignoring patents?
options: File October 2026, launch October 2027
File October 2028, launch October 2030
File October 2026, launch October 2028
File and launch October 2028
questions.explanation: 8 + 2, with no new indication.

questions.prompt: BE was done on the top strength only. What do you ask for?
options: A separate BE study for each strength
A BCS waiver for the top strength
Nothing; one study covers all strengths automatically
The documented biowaiver for the other strengths
questions.explanation: The five conditions must be documented.

questions.prompt: Which part of the dossier will come from the partner whatever the basis?
options: The quality module
The risk management plan only
The reference product's SmPC
The clinical overview only
questions.explanation: Quality always describes your own product.

exercises.scenario: Management asks 'why can't we just launch the day after approval?'

questions.prompt: Which date limits a launch even after approval?
options: The date the bioequivalence study report was signed
The end of market protection, and patents or SPCs
The DCP clock-stop
The end of data protection only
questions.explanation: Launch is the latest of the regulatory and legal dates.

questions.prompt: Which change would add the most months late in a project?
options: Choosing a different wholesaler
Adding a new pack size to the application
Switching from generic to hybrid
Moving the kick-off meeting
questions.explanation: Bridging studies have to be planned, run and reported.

questions.prompt: Explain to a new colleague why the legal basis is one of the first decisions in a project.
questions.modelAnswer: It decides which data the dossier must contain and which it may borrow, and so how long the work before filing will take. Changing it late usually means new studies and months of delay.
